1100.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1100.hook: a woman who is Mom at breakfast and Doctor by nine, and a hymn of names that begins with Mother before it says Queen
1100.howItsDone: Some Hindus, especially in Shakta and Sri Vidya communities, recite the Lalita Sahasranama in full at home or in temples, sometimes offering a flower or a pinch of kumkum with each name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of the Sri Sukta days: the hymn asked Kardama, the mud, to bring the lotus mother home. Today, a new hymn, made of names.
screen: `THE SRI SUKTA.` · `THE LOTUS ASKS THROUGH THE MUD.`

segments.voice: At seven in the morning she's Mom, hunting for a missing shoe. By nine she's Doctor, signing charts. At lunch a friend calls her by a nickname from college. At the temple an old aunty calls her beta, child. Same woman. Every name catches a different side of her, and nobody who loves her would pick just one. Now make that vast. The Lalita Sahasranama is a hymn made almost entirely of names for the goddess, one after another, line after line. Today, how it opens.
screen: `MOM AT SEVEN. DOCTOR BY NINE.` → `EVERY NAME, A DIFFERENT SIDE.` → `A HYMN MADE OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Sahasranama means a thousand names, and Lalita is the goddess they belong to. Tradition places the hymn in the Brahmanda Purana, as a teaching the god Hayagriva gives to the sage Agastya. Some who worship her recite it name by name, at home or in temples. A hymn of names works differently from a story. There's no plot. Each name is a small window, and you look through one, then the next. Over the coming days the path will open a few of those windows, not all of them. So, the first three names, in paraphrase. Sri Mata: the auspicious Mother. Sri Maharajni: the great Queen. Srimat Simhasaneshvari: she who rules from the glorious lion throne. Notice the order. Mother first, before the crown, before the throne, before any of her power is named. Some teachers say that's the key to the whole hymn: whatever she is later, a warrior, a queen, the power behind the universe, she is that as a mother, and the one reciting comes to her as a child. Then the throne, and the lion: royal names, and the lion carries an echo of the fierce goddess the path met in the Devi Mahatmya. And notice the first sound. Sri. The same word the Sri Sukta days were built on: radiance, fortune, the goddess of the lotus. Here it's the opening breath of the very first name. Some readers hear the two hymns meeting there: the fortune of the Sri Sukta becomes the Mother of the thousand names. Others simply hear an auspicious first word, a good way to begin.
screen: `A HYMN MADE OF NAMES.` · `SRI MATA, THE MOTHER.` · `GREAT QUEEN, ON THE LION THRONE.` · `THE FIRST SOUND IS SRI.` · then, large: `MOTHER BEFORE QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Quietly list the names different people call you, the family name, a nickname, the name only one person uses, each on a breath. Then notice which one feels closest to home, and rest there. If you pray, you can say the name you use for God, or for the goddess; if you don't, let your own names be enough.

1101.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1101.hook: the gods at the end of their strength, a fire, and a goddess who rises out of it with work to do
1101.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Lalita Sahasranama before a lamp or a sacred fire, and in Sri Vidya worship the recitation is sometimes joined to fire offerings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama opened with Sri Mata, the Mother, before Queen and throne. Today, two more names, and a fire.

The gods have run out of answers. A demon has the upper hand, and nothing they've tried has worked. So, in the story told around this hymn, they build a great fire and begin a sacrifice. They pour in offerings, and then, when the offerings aren't enough, tradition says they begin to offer themselves. The fire roars higher. And out of the flames a goddess rises: radiant, calm, and already knowing what she's come to do. That is Lalita's arrival. Today, the two names that hold that moment.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE RUN OUT OF ANSWERS.` → `A FIRE, AND A SACRIFICE.` → `OUT OF THE FLAMES, A GODDESS.`

segments.voice: Here are the names, in paraphrase. The fourth: she who was born from the fire-altar of consciousness. The fifth: she who rose up, ready for the work of the gods. Start with the fire. In the story, it's a real sacrifice, an altar with flames. But the name doesn't say a fire of wood. It says a fire of consciousness: chit, awareness itself. So the hymn quietly turns the story inward. Commentators have read that in more than one way. Some say the goddess is born wherever awareness burns clear and steady, so the fire-altar is also the heart of the one who sits and recites. Others keep the story's sense in front: the gods' sacrifice was so total that only something made of pure consciousness could answer it. Either way, notice where she isn't born. Not from a womb, not from a bargain. From a fire. Then the second name, and it's practical. She rose up ready for the work of the gods. She doesn't arrive to be admired; she arrives with a task. The gods had a problem they couldn't solve, and she comes up out of the flames already turned toward the work. Put the two names side by side and you get a small portrait of how this tradition pictures the goddess. Pure awareness, and a job to do. Inner fire, and outer work. Some readers take comfort in that: deep stillness and practical help are not two different goddesses. They're one, rising out of one fire. Tomorrow the hymn turns to what she holds in her hands.

segments.voice: First just notice that you're aware: sounds arrive, the breath moves, a thought passes, and something is knowing it all. Near the end, let one plain question rise out of the stillness, what work is mine today, without forcing an answer. If you pray, you can offer the question to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, let it sit with you.

1102.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1102.hook: a rope, a hook, a sugarcane bow and flower arrows: what the goddess holds, and what the hymn says they are
1102.howItsDone: Devotees of the goddess recite the Lalita Sahasranama at home or in temples, and images of Lalita show her four-armed, holding the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow and the flower arrows the hymn describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama began: the goddess born from the fire-altar of consciousness, risen ready for the work of the gods. Today, her hands.
screen: `BORN FROM THE FIRE OF CONSCIOUSNESS.` → `READY FOR THE WORK.`

segments.voice: A rope. A hook for steering an elephant. A bow cut from sugarcane. Arrows tipped with flowers. That's what the goddess Lalita holds in her four hands, in paintings and temple images. An odd inventory: a noose and a goad sound like tools for catching and driving animals, and a sugarcane bow sounds like something out of a children's story. But the Lalita Sahasranama doesn't leave the objects as objects. A short run of names, early in the hymn, says what each one really is.
screen: `A ROPE, A HOOK, A BOW, ARROWS.` → `AN ODD INVENTORY.` → `FOUR NAMES FOR FOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: After the names of her rising from a fire of consciousness, the hymn describes her form, and four names in a row say what she carries. In paraphrase: she holds the noose that is desire. The Sanskrit there is raga: passion, attachment, the pull toward what we want. She shines with the goad that is anger, the hooked stick that keeps an elephant moving or turns it aside. Her bow of sugarcane is the mind. And her arrows are the five subtle elements, the tanmatras, the subtle forms of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, what the senses meet. Desire, anger, the mind, the senses. The Bhagavad Gita traces how dwelling on things breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger. These are the hard parts of an inner life, and in this hymn they aren't thrown away or trampled. They're in the goddess's hands. Readers take that more than one way. Some say she holds them, so they have no hold on her: the rope that binds a person is, for her, a tool. Others hear something gentler: even a person's desire and anger are not outside her reach. And some notice the sweetness. The mind is a bow, but a bow of sugarcane, and its arrows are flowers. In the old stories Kama, the god of love, carries a sugarcane bow and flower arrows too; the path will come back to him. For today, just the picture: what looks like a rack of weapons turns out to be the inner life, held steady.

Nothing to fix. If you pray, you can offer each to the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let them rest in open hands.

1103.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1103.hook: a war told in names, and the surprising last act after the battle: love brought back from ash
1103.howItsDone: The story of Lalita's war with Bhanda is told in the Lalitopakhyana of the Brahmanda Purana, and devotees who recite the Lalita Sahasranama pass through the battle in a run of its names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama put four things in the goddess's hands: the noose that is desire, the goad that is anger, the bow that is the mind.

What happens to love after it's been burned to ash? In the old stories, Kama, the god of love, once aimed his flower arrows at Shiva in meditation. Shiva opened his third eye, and Kama was burned to nothing. The story told alongside the Lalita Sahasranama picks up from there. Tradition says something grew out of those ashes: a demon named Bhanda, who brought misery to the worlds until the gods offered themselves into a sacrificial fire and the goddess Lalita rose from it. Then comes a war, and the hymn, mostly names, tells the war in names too.
screen: `KAMA BURNED TO ASH.` → `A DEMON FROM THE ASHES.` → `A WAR TOLD IN NAMES.`

segments.voice: Read a stretch slowly and the story moves under the names like a river under ice. In paraphrase: she delights in the courage of her powers as they cut down Bhanda's army. She delights in the young goddess Bala, who strikes down Bhanda's sons. She glances at the face of Kameshvara, her consort, and from that glance Ganesha is formed. She rejoices when Ganesha shatters the device the demons built to block her army. Then the end: with Kameshvara's own weapon she burns Bhanda, and his city with him, and the gods praise her glory. A fine place to finish. But the hymn adds one more name, and it's the surprise. She is the life-giving herb for Kama, who was burned by the fire of Shiva's eye. After the battle, she brings love back. Hold that next to yesterday: Lalita carries the same sugarcane bow and flower arrows Kama carried. The hymn doesn't treat desire as an enemy to destroy forever. What grew wrong out of the ash is defeated, and the one who was burned is restored. Readers take the turn more than one way. Some read it inwardly: the ego's monster is ended, and love, made whole, can live again. Others keep it as story: the goddess is the power who can raise what was turned to ash. And some simply notice the order. The hymn won't let a war be the last word about her. Healing is.
screen: `HER POWERS CUT DOWN BHANDA'S ARMY.` · `GANESHA BREAKS THE BLOCKING DEVICE.` · `BHANDA AND HIS CITY BURN.` · `THEN SHE BRINGS KAMA BACK.` · then, large: `THE LIFE-GIVING HERB FOR KAMA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something in your life that once burned out, a friendship gone quiet, an old enthusiasm, a hope set down, and let it be there like ash after a fire. Without forcing anything, ask what small part of it might still be alive: a memory, a name, one phone number. If you pray, you can bring it before the goddess, or before God, in your own words; if you don't, let the question stay open.

1104.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1104.hook: five things the goddess does, by the hymn's count, and two of them are hiding and grace
1104.howItsDone: In the Shakta reading of the Lalita Sahasranama, the goddess performs the five cosmic acts through the forms of Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Ishvara and Sadashiva; in Shaiva traditions the same five acts are attributed to Shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama told a war in names, and ended it with Kama, love, brought back from ash.

A baby on a kitchen floor, and a grown-up behind a dish towel. The towel goes up, the face is gone, and the baby goes still, a little worried. The towel comes down, there's the face again, and the baby shrieks with laughter. Peekaboo only works because of the hiding: without the moment of not-seeing, there's nothing to find. Today the Lalita Sahasranama does something like it on a cosmic scale. In a short run of names, it lists what the goddess does with the whole universe. Some of it is expected. Two of the acts are not.
screen: `A FACE BEHIND A DISH TOWEL.` → `NO HIDING, NOTHING TO FIND.` → `WHAT SHE DOES WITH THE UNIVERSE.`

segments.voice: Here is the run, in paraphrase. She is the maker, in the form of Brahma. The protector, in the form of Govinda, a name of Vishnu. The one who draws everything back in, in the form of Rudra. The one who conceals, as Ishvara, the Lord. She is Sadashiva, the giver of grace. And a name gathers them up: she is devoted to the five acts. Making, keeping, withdrawing, concealing and grace. Two things stand out. First, the great gods appear as forms the goddess takes. In Shaiva traditions the same five acts belong to Shiva; in this hymn to the goddess they are hers, and the gods are her ways of doing them. Second, the list doesn't stop at endings. After withdrawal comes concealment. The Sanskrit is tirodhana: hiding, veiling. Some teachers who use this list say it's the act that makes the world seem to be only itself, so the deeper reality behind it is out of sight. That sounds unkind until you remember the dish towel. Then the last act: anugraha, grace, favor, the turning toward someone. The towel coming down. Some readers take the order seriously: concealing comes before grace, the way hiding comes before finding. Others say the five aren't a sequence at all, but five things happening at once, in every moment. Either way, the hymn puts something startling in plain sight. The one who hides is the same one who reveals.
screen: `MAKING, KEEPING, WITHDRAWING.` · `THE GODS AS HER FORMS.` · `CONCEALING: TIRODHANA.` · `GRACE: ANUGRAHA.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO HIDES IS THE ONE WHO REVEALS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes for a few breaths and let the room be concealed: the chair, the walls, the light are all still there, you just can't see them. Then slowly open your eyes and let the room come back, as if it were being handed to you; close them and rest, open them and receive, each opening unhurried. If you pray, you can greet the goddess in what returns, in your own words; if you don't, just notice what it's like to be given the room again.

1105.hook: the goddess has a jeweled city, and then the hymn gives her a second address: inside the body
1105.howItsDone: In Shakta Tantra and the Sri Vidya tradition, the kundalini names of the Lalita Sahasranama are read as a map of inner practice taught by a guru; other devotees simply recite them as praise of the goddess within.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama named the goddess's five acts: making, keeping, withdrawing, concealing and grace.

Same goddess, two addresses. Early in the Lalita Sahasranama she lives somewhere grand. The names place her in the middle of an ocean of nectar, in a forest of kadamba trees, in a house of wish-granting gems, seated on a throne. A palace you'd need a map to find. Then, further on, the hymn turns and gives her a second address, and this one isn't far away at all. It's a human body, starting at the base of the spine.
screen: `AN OCEAN OF NECTAR, A HOUSE OF GEMS.` → `THEN A SECOND ADDRESS.` → `INSIDE A HUMAN BODY.`

segments.voice: Here is the run, in paraphrase, and it moves like a climb. Her one dwelling is the muladhara, the root center at the base of the spine. She pierces the knot of Brahma. She rises within the manipura, the center at the navel. She pierces the knot of Vishnu. She stands within the ajna, the center between the brows. She pierces the knot of Rudra. She rises onto the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, and from there she pours down streams of nectar. A few names on, the hymn calls her bright as a streak of lightning, dwelling above the six centers, and names her outright: Kundalini, the coiled one, fine as the thread inside a lotus stalk. So the queen of the jeweled city is also a power curled at the root of a human body, rising, untying knots and raining nectar back down. In Shakta Tantra and in the Sri Vidya tradition these names are read as a map for inner practice, and those practices are taught by a teacher, in person, with care. This path doesn't teach them. Others hear the names devotionally: the goddess isn't only out there. And some readers notice the three knots. Each carries the name of a great god, Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, and the goddess passes through all three. What looked like a palace far away turns out to have a door much closer in.
screen: `FROM THE ROOT OF THE SPINE.` · `THROUGH THREE KNOTS.` · `TO THE LOTUS AT THE CROWN.` · `KUNDALINI, THE COILED ONE.` · then, large: `A DOOR MUCH CLOSER IN.`

segments.voice: Sit tall without strain and feel where you meet the chair or the floor, the base of the spine, solid and supported; then let attention move slowly to the belly rising and falling, to the space between the brows, to the crown of the head. No pushing, no picturing energy, just noticing, place by place, the way you'd walk up a staircase in your own house. If you pray, you can greet the goddess at each step; if you don't, let the climb be quiet.
The Lalita Sahasranama. Today, the names that give the goddess a second home: rising from the root of the spine to the lotus at the crown.

1106.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1106.hook: soon after names that say devotion can win her, a run of names that say she is without form, without qualities, without parts
1106.howItsDone: Devotees reciting the Lalita Sahasranama pass from names that praise her form and her closeness to devotees into names that call her formless and beyond qualities, and different Hindu schools explain the relation of saguna and nirguna in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama gave the goddess a second address: rising from the root of the spine to the lotus at the crown. Today closes a week.

Sanskrit has a small prefix, nir, that works a lot like the English word without. Put it in front of a word and the word turns inside out. In the Lalita Sahasranama there's a stretch where name after name begins that way: without support, without stain, without form. What makes the run startling is what comes just before it. A few names earlier, the hymn has been saying the warmest things about her: how close she is, how easily she's reached.
screen: `NIR: A LOT LIKE WITHOUT.` → `NAME AFTER NAME.` → `NEARNESS, AND WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: First, the nearness. In paraphrase: she is fond of devotion, reached through devotion, won over by devotion, and she is the one who takes fear away. A goddess you could talk to across a kitchen table. Then, a little further on, the other run. Without support, needing nothing to stand on. Stainless. Untouched by anything. Pure. Eternal. Without form. Without agitation. Without qualities, nirguna. Without parts. Peaceful. Without desire. Read them aloud and the earlier pictures fall away: the four hands, the jeweled city, the throne. The hymn that painted her face now says she has no form at all. Hindu thinkers have names for these two ways of speaking. Saguna: with qualities, the goddess you can see, praise and love. Nirguna: beyond qualities, the reality no picture can hold. Teachers in different schools weigh the two differently. Some say the formless is the deeper truth and the forms are a kindness to us. Others say the form is no lesser thing, that she is fully present in it. The hymn doesn't stop to settle it. It keeps both in the same breath. And notice one name in the run: without desire. Four days ago, desire was the noose in her hand. The hymn is happy to say both. That fits the week. It opened with the mother and the fire, put the inner life in her hands, told a war that ended in love restored, named her five acts and gave her a home in the body. Now, at the week's end, it says no address can hold her.
screen: `WON OVER BY DEVOTION.` · `WITHOUT FORM, WITHOUT QUALITIES.` · `SAGUNA AND NIRGUNA.` · `BOTH IN THE SAME BREATH.` · then, large: `NO ADDRESS CAN HOLD HER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a face, an image or a word that feels close to you, something you could speak to, and let it be near; then gently let the picture go and stay with what's left, the breath, the quiet, the room. Let the picture come back if it wants to, and move between the two without choosing. If you pray, you can rest with the goddess, or with God, in either way; if you don't, simply notice the difference.
The Lalita Sahasranama. Today, names of nearness, won over by devotion, and names of without: without form, without qualities, without parts.
